# Abstract

Between the close of the Late Pleistocene in 10000BC and the twilight of the Toltec era in 1200AD, the lands of central, western, Gulf and northern Mexico moved from sparse foraging bands to some of the densest pre-industrial urban states in the Americas. Spanning seven biophysical sub-regions and 1.786.174 km² across Mexico outside the lowland Maya east, our gridded Holocene demographic substratum expands 6,71-fold from 241,2k inhabitants (0,14 inhabitants per km²) in 10000BC to 998,2k in 3000BC, reaches a Formative substratum ridge of 1,74M in 1000BC, resets across the Common-Era raster seam to 919,3k at 1AD and 959,2k in 600AD and climbs to 1,62M (0,91 inhabitants per km²) by 1200AD [@Gonzalezmartin2015Demographic; @SandersParsonsSantley1979]. Archaeological pedestrian surveys across the Mesoamerican agrarian core reveal a still steeper demographic ascent once urban compounds and rural hamlets are summed directly, rising from roughly 120k foragers in 10000BC and 1,42M Formative villagers in 1000BC to 4,93M in 600AD and 6,65M by 1200AD [@Cowgill2015; @Blanton1999; @Pool2007]. Throughout these eleven millennia, human geography pivoted from alluvial wetlands and dry highland rock shelters toward intensively farmed basins: Archaic squash and maize domestication in Oaxaca and Tehuacán laid the basis for Early Formative Olmec centres along the Gulf littoral at San Lorenzo (10,8k) and La Venta (11,4k), hilltop state nucleation at Monte Albán (24,9k) in Oaxaca, metropolitan concentration at Cuicuilco (19,8k) and Teotihuacán (124k) in the Basin of Mexico, Epiclassic realignment across Cantona (79,4k), Cholula (33,2k), El Tajín (19,8k), Xochicalco (15,6k) and Cacaxtla-Xochitécatl (11,4k) and Early Post-Classic urbanism at Tula (56,4k) [@Diehl2004; @Healan2012]. By 1200AD, gridded sub-regional densities ranged more than threefold from 1,84 inhabitants per km² in the Gulf Olmec and Veracruz Lowlands, 1,61 in Oaxaca and Mixteca and 1,59 in the Basin of Mexico down to 0,54 across the Arid Northern Interior and Baja California, while 336 catalogued archaeological settlements display a mature rank-size slope ($\alpha = 1,09$, $R^2 = 0,88$) that separates Mexico's early cities from its sparse arid northern frontier.

# Background

## Archaic Foragers and the Domestication of Maize (10000BC to 2000BC)

At the close of the Younger Dryas around 10000BC, Mexico was a sparsely peopled mosaic of arid northern basins, volcanic central plateaux and humid tropical lowlands. Genetic coalescence models derived from indigenous Mesoamerican mitochondrial DNA indicate that after initial Late Pleistocene entry into the Americas, human numbers expanded rapidly once Holocene climates warmed and stabilised, establishing distinct regional maternal lineages across highland and coastal corridors [@Gonzalezmartin2015Demographic]. Yet for the first five millennia of the Holocene, subsistence remained mobile. Small macro-bands of 20 to 60 people moved seasonally between highland dry caves, lacustrine marshes and Pacific or Gulf estuaries, harvesting agave, prickly pear, mesquite pods, waterfowl, deer and small game.

The archaeological anchors of this Archaic world are few but unusually informative. On Baja California's Pacific margin, coastal foragers occupied Isla Cedros by 9000BC and Espíritu Santo Island by 6500BC, exploiting marine shellfish and sea mammals far beyond any agricultural frontier. Inland, stratified dry rock shelters in the semi-arid rain shadows of southern Mexico recorded one of the decisive agricultural transitions in human history. At Guilá Naquitz in the eastern Valley of Oaxaca and Coxcatlán Cave in the Tehuacán Valley (both active from 8500BC in our settlement register), followed by open-air seasonal camps such as Gheo-Shih (5500BC) and lacustrine settlements at Tlapacoya (5000BC) on the shore of Lake Chalco, Archaic foragers began selecting bottle gourds, *Cucurbita pepo* squash, beans and wild teosinte (*Zea mays* ssp. *parviglumis*) along the Balsas-Oaxaca-Tehuacán arc [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Kowalewski1989].

Maize did not transform Mesoamerican demography overnight. For more than two millennia after initial cob domestication around 7000BC to 5000BC, early ears were barely thumb-sized, serving as a reliable storable supplement rather than a staple capable of anchoring permanent villages. Across the gridded Holocene substratum, total population across Mexico rises from 241,2k in 10000BC to 727,6k in 6000BC before dipping to 491,9k in 5000BC during mid-Holocene arid pulses, then climbing steadily to 998,2k by 3000BC and 1,1M by 2000BC as larger-cobbed maize varieties spread into alluvial river valleys. Only when higher-yielding cobs combined with ceramic cooking vessels around 2000BC to 1600BC did mobile foraging circuits snap shut into year-round sedentary hamlets [@Pool2007; @Diehl2004].

## Gulf Olmec Centres and Formative Lowland Nucleation (1600BC to 400BC)

The first unmistakable surge toward monumental civic scale occurred not in the volcanic central highlands, but along the humid alluvial floodplains of southern Veracruz and western Tabasco. There, rich natural levees along the Coatzacoalcos, Tonalá and Papaloapan rivers yielded two maize harvests a year alongside abundant riverine fish, turtles, manatees and palm fruits [@Diehl2004; @Pool2007]. Because levee soils were circumscribed by seasonally flooded backswamps, control over elevated farming land created steep local wealth gradients early in the Formative period.

San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán rose on a sculpted riverine plateau above the Coatzacoalcos basin between 1400BC and 1000BC, reaching an estimated 10,8k inhabitants at its peak around 1000BC while its surrounding Capoacan hinterland absorbed dispersed farming hamlets into a multi-tier local hierarchy [@Diehl2004; @Baizabal2019Asentamiento]. Its rulers mobilised labour across dozens of kilometres to haul multi-tonne basalt boulders from the Tuxtla Mountains for colossal portrait heads and basalt drains. Across adjacent tributary corridors such as Medias Aguas, pedestrian surveys trace how Formative communities clustered tightly along elevated terraces overlooking floodplains, adjusting settlement locations repeatedly as river channels avulsed [@Reyes2019Patro]. Even in recent demographic studies of southern Veracruz, the ecological contrast between productive river bottoms and marginal uplands continues to govern rural mobility and internal migration gradients [@Contributors2007Determinants].

After San Lorenzo declined around 900BC, demographic and ceremonial leadership shifted eastward to La Venta on a salt-dome island amidst the Tonalá wetlands of Tabasco. Between 900BC and 400BC, La Venta reached 11,4k inhabitants at its 600BC zenith, raising Mesoamerica's earliest great earthen pyramid and burying massive serpentine pavement offerings before political fragmentation scattered its population [@Pool2007; @Diehl2004]. Farther west near the Tuxtla piedmont, Tres Zapotes (peaking at 7,9k in 200AD) and Laguna de los Cerros sustained Epi-Olmec civic continuity well into the Classic period, bridging Formative Gulf traditions with Long Count calendrics and highland trade networks [@Pool2007].

## Oaxaca Valley Consolidation and the Rise of Monte Albán (1500BC to 750AD)

While Olmec rulers commanded the Gulf levees, a distinct highland path to urban statehood unfolded in the three-armed Valley of Oaxaca (Etla, Tlacolula and Valle Grande). Bounded by steep sierra walls and blessed with a high water table permitting simple pot-irrigation (*riego a brazo*), the valley floor supported Early Formative villages led by San José Mogote in the Etla arm [@Blanton1999; @Kowalewski1989]. Agent-based demographic simulations confirm that topographic circumscription inside this semi-arid highland basin amplified competition over irrigable alluvium once village densities crossed local thresholds, favouring defensive coalition-building over further village fissioning [@Williams2025Testing].

Around 500BC, leaders from rival valley arms founded Monte Albán atop a rugged, artificially levelled mountain massif rising 400 m above the central valley junction. The choice was deliberately defensive and politically neutral, yet it imposed severe logistical hurdles because the summit lacked perennial springs. Zapotec engineers solved the water constraint through an integrated network of stone check dams, drainage canals, catch basins and household cisterns that captured summer storm runoff across the terraced flanks, enabling the hilltop capital to climb from 5,3k inhabitants in 450BC to 14,9k in 200BC and 24,9k at its 650AD Classic apogee [@Blanton1999; @Gracida2019Studying]. Strontium isotope baselines constructed across the Valley of Oaxaca show how radiogenic geological variation between the valley arms and surrounding sierras allows direct reconstruction of immigration into the capital and its hinterland [@Pachecofores2025Radiogenic].

Monte Albán never stood alone. Across the surrounding arms of the valley and into the upland Mixteca Alta, secondary centres such as Yucuita, Huamelulpan, Yucunudahui, Dainzú, Lambityeco and Ejutla anchored regional market and terrace economies [@Kowalewski1989; @Geurds2008Grounding]. To the south across the Sierra Sur and toward the Pacific coast at Río Viejo, Late Formative hilltop centres maintained persistent local identities that outlasted Monte Albán's eighth-century political decentralisation [@Zborover2014Decolonizing]. As Monte Albán shrank from 24,9k in 650AD to 8,8k in 850AD and 4,2k by 1100AD, population did not vanish from Oaxaca; instead it re-aggregated into competing valley-floor and piedmont capitals including Jalieza (peaking at 16,2k in 950AD), Zaachila (9,6k by 1200AD), Mitla (8,9k by 1200AD) and Yagul (6,9k in 1150AD) [@Kowalewski1989; @Blanton1999].

## Basin of Mexico Nucleation and Teotihuacán's Zenith (800BC to 650AD)

Nowhere in Mesoamerica did demographic concentration reach the sheer magnitude witnessed in the Basin of Mexico. At 2.240 m elevation, this endorheic highland bowl of lakes and fertile volcanic piedmonts experienced relatively modest Middle Formative settlement until lakeside agriculture and early canal irrigation unlocked southern Lake Chalco-Xochimilco [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Carballo2016]. By the Late Formative, two rival regional capitals emerged at opposite ends of the basin: Cuicuilco on the lush southwestern shore (reaching 19,8k inhabitants by 150BC) and Teotihuacán in the drier northeastern spring-fed valley.

Volcanic catastrophe tipped the balance decisively. Successive eruptions of Popocatépetl around 50AD devastated the western Puebla slopes (burying farming villages such as Tetimpa and reshaping Cholula's Formative trajectory), while the eruption of the Xitle cinder cone buried Cuicuilco's agricultural lands beneath thick pedregal basalt [@PlunketUrunuela2012; @SandersParsonsSantley1979]. Refugees poured northward into the Teotihuacán Valley. Between 100BC and 250AD, Teotihuacán exploded from 28,5k to 96k inhabitants, draining much of the surrounding Basin of Mexico rural countryside into a single planned grid city of roughly 20 km² [@Millon1973; @Cowgill2015].

At its Classic zenith around 450AD, Teotihuacán housed approximately 124k inhabitants (within the scholarly range of 80k to 125k), making it the largest city in the Western Hemisphere and among the six largest on earth [@Millon1973; @Cowgill2015]. Unlike sprawling low-density tropical capitals, Teotihuacán housed the bulk of its citizens inside roughly 2.000 walled, single-storey stone-and-plaster apartment compounds arranged along a rigid orthogonal street grid centred on the Avenue of the Dead [@Millon1973; @Carballo2010Advances]. Ancient mitochondrial DNA from Classic Teotihuacán burials confirms high genetic diversity consistent with continuous immigration from across Mesoamerica, matching archaeological neighbourhoods of Zapotec, Gulf Coast and West Mexican artisans [@Aguirresamudio2017Genetic; @Cowgill2015]. Feeding and ritualising a metropolis of 124k without draught animals or wheeled carts required extraordinary urban provisioning: stable isotope analyses of cottontail and jackrabbit bone mineral from residential compounds reveal intensive maize-fed rabbit husbandry for urban protein [@Somerville2016Animal], while isotopic signatures from captive pumas, jaguars, wolves and golden eagles interred inside the Moon and Feathered Serpent pyramids demonstrate state-organised feeding of apex predators on maize-consuming prey [@Sugiyama2015Stable]. Teotihuacán's commercial and diplomatic reach stretched from Chingú in Hidalgo (7,2k) to Matacapan in the Tuxtla Mountains of Veracruz (14,6k) and deep into the Maya highlands [@Cowgill2015; @Carballo2016].

## Epiclassic Realignment, West Mexico and the Toltec Horizon (650AD to 1200AD)

Sometime around 550AD to 650AD, a systematic conflagration destroyed the civic palaces and temples along Teotihuacán's Avenue of the Dead. Population plunged from 124k in 450AD and 108k in 550AD down to 39,5k in 650AD and 24,2k by 800AD, ending seven centuries of highland unipolarity [@Cowgill2015; @SandersParsonsSantley1979]. What followed during the Epiclassic (650AD to 900AD) was not demographic collapse across Mexico as a whole, but an energetic, militarised multipolar dispersal into fortified hilltop and volcanic-flow capitals ringing the Central Highlands and Gulf piedmont [@Carballo2016].

East of the basin on an arid malpaís lava flow controlling obsidian quarries, Cantona surged to 79,4k inhabitants by 800AD, packing thousands of walled residential patios and 24 ballcourts onto defensible basalt ridges. In the Puebla-Tlaxcala valley, Cholula weathered Classic disruption to reach 33,2k by 1100AD around its immense adobe Great Pyramid, while fortified Cacaxtla-Xochitécatl (11,4k in 700AD) dominated the Atoyac corridor with Maya-influenced polychrome murals [@PlunketUrunuela2012; @Carballo2016]. South of the basin in Morelos, Xochicalco fortified a terraced hilltop to reach 15,6k by 800AD, while to the west Teotenango (9,4k) guarded the Toluca valley. Along the central Gulf coast, El Tajín expanded rapidly to 19,8k by 850AD as the premier ceremonial capital of Classic Veracruz, flanked by El Pital (9,6k), Cerro de las Mesas (8,4k) and early Cempoala (9,9k by 1200AD). Across Mesoamerica's southeastern borderlands, osteological palaeodemography at Late and Terminal Classic centres registers mounting nutritional stress and demographic volatility during this same eighth-to-tenth-century restructuring [@Morfin2013Mayas].

West of the central volcanic highlands, the Santiago-Balsas and Michoacán lake basins followed an independent trajectory rooted in shaft-tomb ceremonialism and circular terraced pyramids (*guachimontones*). Centred on the Tequila volcanoes of Jalisco, the Teuchitlán polity peaked around 400AD at 22,4k inhabitants in its core Guachimontones complex, sustained by raised wetland fields (*chinampas* around Lake Magdalena) and obsidian extraction, before declining after 650AD as Loma Alta in the Zacapu marsh (7,6k), Ixtlán del Río (6,9k), El Chanal (5,9k) and terraced agricultural landscapes around Lake Pátzcuaro rose toward Post-Classic prominence [@Pezzutti2007Steps]. Farther north along the arid frontier of the Bajío, Querétaro and Zacatecas, agrarian expansion during wetter Classic centuries pushed Mesoamerican colonists out to El Cerrito (6,9k), La Quemada (4,9k), Alta Vista Chalchihuites and La Ferrería, before late first-millennium drying pulled the farming frontier back southward [@Mastache2002].

Those southward-migrating Bajío farmers converged with Central Highland survivors in the semi-arid Tula Valley of Hidalgo to forge the Early Post-Classic Toltec state. Growing from Tula Chico (4,6k in 700AD and 19,2k in 850AD) into sprawling Tula Grande covering 16 km², Tula reached 56,4k inhabitants around 1000AD and maintained 44,8k at 1150AD, integrating obsidian blade manufacture, lime production and long-distance turquoise and Gulf trade [@Mastache2002; @Healan2012]. Surrounding Basin of Mexico towns such as Tizayuca preserved household subsistence complexes blending maize agriculture with specialised domestic dog breeding [@Manin2018Identify], while southern lakeshore city-states at Chalco (14,9k) and Culhuacán (9,4k) expanded rapidly as Tula suffered internal burning and abandonment in the late twelfth century [@Healan2012; @SandersParsonsSantley1979]. By our closing horizon of 1200AD, central and western Mexico stood poised on the threshold of the Late Post-Classic city-state boom that would culminate in the Aztec Triple Alliance and the Tarascan Empire.

# Methodology

## Biophysical Partition of Seven Mesoamerican and Aridoamerican Sub-Regions

Pre-Columbian Mexico knew no modern federal states, and imposing twenty-first-century state borders onto Archaic foragers or Formative states distorts every watershed and ecological gradient. JAGUAR therefore partitions Mexico outside the Maya Yucatán-Chiapas lowlands into seven biophysical sub-regions derived from Level-6 HydroBASINS catchments and archaeological culture-area boundaries, totalling 1.786.173,6 km² across 22.958 raster cells.

Four sub-regions form the densely settled Mesoamerican agrarian core, occupying just 26,3% of total land area (469.197,4 km²) yet generating the great bulk of monumental urbanism and pedestrian survey coverage. The Basin of Mexico and Central Highlands (147.967,1 km²) unites the endorheic Valley of Mexico with Puebla-Tlaxcala, Morelos, Toluca and southern Hidalgo. The Gulf Olmec and Veracruz Lowlands (125.755,7 km²) encompasses the humid littoral from the Huasteca and Papaloapan south to the Coatzacoalcos and Tonalá floodplains. Oaxaca and Mixteca Sierra-Valleys (60.535,6 km²) groups the Valley of Oaxaca, Mixteca Alta, Cañada and adjacent Pacific coast. West Mexico Santiago-Balsas (134.939 km²) spans Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit, Michoacán and the middle Balsas corridor.

The remaining three sub-regions encompass 73,7% of land area (1.316.976,2 km²) across Mexico's semi-arid transitional frontier and arid north. The Bajío and North-Central Highlands (285.316,5 km²) tracks the fluctuating agrarian frontier across Guanajuato, Querétaro, San Luis Potosí, Zacatecas and southern Durango where Classic Mesoamerican towns expanded and later retreated. Pacific Sierra Madre and Sonora-Sinaloa (83.542,3 km²) captures the coastal river plains of Sinaloa and southern Sonora anchored by early Aztatlán complexes. Finally, the Arid Northern Interior and Baja California (948.117,4 km², 53,1% of the entire chapter domain) covers the Chihuahuan and Sonoran deserts, Sierra Madre Occidental interior and Baja peninsula, where sparse foraging and desert-oases farming prevailed until after 1200AD.

## Dual Substratum Kriging and Archaeological Survey Calibration

Reconstructing Pre-Columbian headcounts across eleven millennia without historical tax censuses requires reconciling two fundamentally different classes of quantitative evidence: continuous gridded Holocene land-use rasters and bottom-up archaeological pedestrian surveys [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Kowalewski1989; @Carballo2010Advances]. For each biophysical sub-region $r$ of terrestrial area $A_r$ at benchmark year $t \in [-10000, 1200]$, the chapter summary cache extracts gridded substratum population $P_r^{\mathrm{grid}}(t)$ by masking continuous Holocene raster surfaces with the seven-colour areal mask and summing cell values inside each polygon:

$$P_r^{\mathrm{grid}}(t) = \sum_{c \in \Omega_r} \rho_c(t) \cdot a_c$$

where $\Omega_r$ is the set of raster cells belonging to sub-region $r$, $\rho_c(t)$ is the kriged population density of cell $c$ at year $t$ and $a_c$ is the geodesic cell area in km². Effective gridded density follows directly as $d_r^{\mathrm{grid}}(t) = P_r^{\mathrm{grid}}(t) / A_r$.

Because global Holocene land-use rasters distribute substantial background population smoothly across vast arid catchments and exhibit a structural discontinuity across the 1000BC to 100AD transition between prehistoric and Common-Era raster series, JAGUAR pairs the gridded substratum with an independent archaeological survey calibration series $P_r^{\mathrm{arch}}(t)$ compiled from regional full-coverage surveys. In the Basin of Mexico, Valley of Oaxaca, Teotihuacán Valley, Puebla-Tlaxcala and Tula heartland, archaeologists estimate local site population $N_s(t)$ from mapped habitation area $H_s(t)$, surface sherd density multipliers $m_s$ and excavated house-compound counts [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Millon1973; @Kowalewski1989; @Carballo2010Advances]:

$$N_s(t) = H_s(t) \cdot m_s(t) \cdot \gamma_{\mathrm{occ}}$$

where $m_s(t)$ scales from 5 to 10 persons per hectare in dispersed Formative hamlets up to 50 to 80 persons per hectare in walled Teotihuacán apartment compounds, and $\gamma_{\mathrm{occ}} \in [0,7, 0,9]$ accounts for simultaneous house occupancy within a ceramic phase [@Cowgill2015; @Carballo2010Advances]. Similar settlement-catchment methods developed along the southern Gulf-Maya borderlands around Palenque and the Michoacán terraced basins of Lake Pátzcuaro calibrate rural hinterland ratios outside the central plateaux [@Stuardo2005Archaeological; @Pezzutti2007Steps]. Meanwhile, strontium isoscape models and environmental circumscription simulations constrain inter-valley migration flows so urban surges at Monte Albán or Teotihuacán balance against rural depopulation in adjacent catchment rings [@Pachecofores2025Radiogenic; @Williams2025Testing].

## Settlement Gazetteer Assembly and Rank-Size Formalism

Alongside regional area series, JAGUAR assembles a geocoded gazetteer of 336 Pre-Columbian settlements across Mexico active between 9000BC and 1200AD. Four sequential ingestion waves recorded in the chapter source ledger reached empirical saturation at a final marginal gain of 0,9%: Wave 1 ingested 306 settlements from primary archaeological survey corpora led by the Arizona State University Basin of Mexico Settlement Persistence Dataset and full-coverage Valley of Oaxaca, Teotihuacán and Tula registers; Wave 2 added 22 regional entries from peer-reviewed regional monographs across Veracruz, West Mexico and northern frontiers (7,19% marginal gain); Wave 3 backfilled 5 longitudinal Archaic and Formative sites (1,52% marginal gain); and Wave 4 added 3 sub-regional gap closures (0,9% marginal gain), leaving 0 excluded duplicates and a 0% crowd-sourced fallback share.

To quantify urban hierarchy maturation across all 336 catalogued city-proper sites, peak settlement sizes $S_{(k)}$ ordered by descending rank $k$ are fitted across the upper half of the distribution (168 settlements) using the standard log-linear rank-size power law:

$$\log_{10} S_{(k)} = \log_{10} S_1 - \alpha \log_{10} k$$

where $\alpha = 1$ denotes a classic Zipfian integrated urban hierarchy, $\alpha < 0,7$ marks a flat pre-urban village landscape and $\alpha > 1,1$ signals a primate-heavy metropolitan system dominated by imperial capitals such as Teotihuacán or Cantona.

# Testing and Validation

## Reconciling Gridded Substrata with Archaeological Pedestrian Surveys

A central diagnostic test of Pre-Columbian demography is confronting continuous global raster substrata against full-coverage archaeological field surveys. Across the 1.786.174 km² Mexican study domain, the two series agree closely in order of magnitude during the Formative millennium (1,74M gridded versus 1,42M archaeological in 1000BC), but diverge sharply after 1AD for two transparent structural reasons. First, the gridded substratum exhibits a marked seam drop from 1,74M in 1000BC down to 919,3k in 1AD and 619,4k in 100AD before climbing back to 959,2k in 600AD and 1,62M in 1200AD, reflecting the underlying splice between prehistoric and Common-Era global hindcast rasters. Second, global rasters spread population proportionally across Mexico's vast northern arid basin (allocating 513,8k, or 31,7% of the entire 1200AD domain total, to the 948.117 km² Arid Northern Interior and Baja California), whereas archaeological field surveys place the overwhelming majority of Classic and Early Post-Classic inhabitants inside the four humid and volcanic Mesoamerican basins (5,61M of 6,65M, or 84,4%, by 1200AD) [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Cowgill2015; @Kowalewski1989].

Table \ref{tab:subregion-trajectories} reports the gridded sub-regional trajectory extracted directly from the chapter summary cache across six key chronological milestones from 10000BC to 1200AD, matching the series rendered in Figure \ref{fig:meso-trajectory}.

To benchmark these raster totals against ground-level archaeology, Table \ref{tab:arch-comparison} juxtaposes 1200AD gridded headcounts against the archaeological pedestrian-survey calibration envelope and catalogued site recovery intensity per 10.000 km². In the Basin of Mexico and Central Highlands, where Teotihuacán alone reached 124k in 450AD and Cantona, Tula and Cholula collectively exceeded 169k at their respective peaks, pedestrian surveys support roughly 1,85M inhabitants in 600AD and 2,45M by 1200AD (16,69 inhabitants per km²) — ten times higher than the uncalibrated raster average of 1,59 inhabitants per km² [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Cowgill2015; @Carballo2010Advances]. Conversely, in the Arid Northern Interior and Baja California, archaeological evidence points to roughly 240k inhabitants (0,26 inhabitants per km²) by 1200AD, less than half the raster's 513,8k allocation. Reporting both figures side by side prevents either source of distortion from masquerading as settled fact.

## Historical GIS Sub-Administrative Regimes and Bioarchaeological Checks

A second cross-check evaluates the 23 sub-administrative polygon records scraped from the historical GIS regime stack at 1AD, 500AD and 1000AD (Table \ref{tab:hgis-subadmin}). At 1AD and 500AD, the de jure polity layer maps the Zapotec state across 71.004 km² at 143,6k inhabitants (2,02 inhabitants per km²), while a tighter de facto core polygon at 500AD encloses 129,6k across 14.572 km² (8,89 inhabitants per km²), neatly bracketing the Monte Albán IIIB regional survey core [@Blanton1999; @Kowalewski1989]. By 1000AD, the de facto fallback layer registers the Toltec sphere across 462.874 km² at 1,14M inhabitants (2,45 inhabitants per km²), capturing Tula's hegemonic arc across Hidalgo, the northern Basin of Mexico and the southern Bajío [@Mastache2002; @Healan2012].

Independent bioarchaeological and isotopic evidence confirms the scale and urban mechanics of these highland estimates. At Teotihuacán, burial mtDNA lineages demonstrate continuous demographic inflow from outside the valley [@Aguirresamudio2017Genetic], while stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes from domestic leporids and ritual carnivores show that maize surplus supported both everyday protein husbandry and state ceremonies inside dense multi-family compounds [@Somerville2016Animal; @Sugiyama2015Stable]. In Oaxaca, hydraulic calculations for Monte Albán's cisterns and check dams verify the water supply needed to sustain 20k to 25k residents atop an arid mountain ridge [@Gracida2019Studying], while radiogenic strontium isoscapes differentiate local Etla-Tlacolula villagers from sierra migrants [@Pachecofores2025Radiogenic]. Along the Gulf rim and Maya borderlands, settlement-density transects around Capoacan, Medias Aguas and Palenque confirm that lowland agrarian centres maintained broader garden-city footprints than highland stone grids, while osteological mortality profiles from Late and Terminal Classic skeletal series document elevated childhood stress during the eighth-to-tenth-century political transitions [@Baizabal2019Asentamiento; @Stuardo2005Archaeological; @Morfin2013Mayas].

# Results

## Long-Run Demographic Trajectory across Highland, Gulf and Northern Mexico

Figure \ref{fig:meso-trajectory} plots the continuous gridded demographic curve across all seven biophysical sub-regions from 10000BC to 1200AD (Panel A) alongside final 1200AD regional density rankings (Panel B). Across eleven millennia, aggregate gridded population expanded 6,71-fold from 241,2k in 10000BC to 1,62M in 1200AD, lifting mean domain density from 0,14 to 0,91 inhabitants per km². Four distinct structural phases stand out in the time series.

<figure class="crd-figure-block" id="fig:meso-trajectory">
<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_jaguar/1.0-precolumbian-mesoamerica/precolumbian_mesoamerica_population_trajectory.png" alt="fig:meso-trajectory" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 2.</span> Gridded population trajectory for Pre-Columbian Mexico and its four largest sub-regions from 10000BC to 1200AD (Panel A) and sub-regional population density rankings in 1200AD (Panel B).</figcaption>
</figure>

During the Early-to-Mid Holocene Archaic phase (10000BC to 5000BC), gridded numbers climbed from 241,2k in 10000BC to 333,4k in 8000BC and 727,6k in 6000BC before contracting to 491,9k in 5000BC during mid-Holocene drying. Throughout these millennia, regional shares tracked raw territorial area rather than agricultural intensity: the immense Arid Northern Interior and Baja California (53,1% of land area) held 44,7% of gridded population in 10000BC (107,8k), followed by the Bajío and North-Central Highlands at 23,5% (56,8k), whereas the Basin of Mexico held just 5,6% (13,5k) and Oaxaca 2,4% (5,7k).

Between 4000BC and 1000BC, sedentary maize-bean-squash farming shifted demographic gravity decisively southward. Aggregate gridded population nearly tripled from 622,2k in 4000BC to 998,2k in 3000BC, 1,1M in 2000BC and 1,74M in 1000BC, while the four Mesoamerican core basins jumped from 24,8% of domain population in 10000BC to 51,7% (900,1k) by 1000BC. The Gulf Olmec and Veracruz Lowlands surged 16-fold from 21k in 10000BC to 337,9k in 1000BC (19,4% of all Mexico), mirroring the golden age of San Lorenzo and La Venta [@Diehl2004; @Pool2007]. Across the archaeological survey envelope, the same transition lifted total headcounts from 490k in 3000BC to 1,42M in 1000BC.

Across the Formative-Classic transition (1000BC to 600AD), the gridded substratum dips across the 1AD to 100AD raster seam to 619,4k before expanding steadily through the Classic era to 747,4k in 400AD, 857,4k in 500AD and 959,2k in 600AD. In the archaeological survey record, this exact window witnessed Mexico's single steepest urban leap, carrying total population from 1,42M in 1000BC to 2,79M in 1AD and 4,93M in 600AD as Teotihuacán, Monte Albán, Cholula and Teuchitlán nucleated entire valleys [@Cowgill2015; @Blanton1999; @PlunketUrunuela2012].

Finally, between 700AD and 1200AD, both series record vigorous post-Teotihuacán demographic recovery and expansion. After a modest seventh-century hesitation (from 959,2k in 600AD to 919,2k in 700AD matching Teotihuacán's fall), gridded population crossed 1,02M in 800AD, 1,06M in 900AD, 1,26M in 1000AD, 1,3M in 1100AD and 1,62M in 1200AD, while the archaeological survey series climbed from 4,93M in 600AD to 6,65M in 1200AD. By 1200AD, gridded sub-regional densities arranged themselves along a clean ecological gradient from tropical and highland agrarian cores to arid northern deserts: Gulf Olmec and Veracruz Lowlands led at 1,84 inhabitants per km², followed by Oaxaca and Mixteca at 1,61, the Basin of Mexico and Central Highlands at 1,59, West Mexico Santiago-Balsas at 1,35, the Bajío and North-Central Highlands at 1,01, Pacific Sierra Madre and Sonora-Sinaloa at 0,83 and the Arid Northern Interior and Baja California at 0,54.

## Basin of Mexico and Central Highlands: Unipolar Metropolis to Multipolar States

Covering 147.967,1 km² (8,3% of the chapter domain), the Basin of Mexico and Central Highlands recorded the steepest eleven-millennium proportional growth in the gridded substratum, multiplying 17,5-fold from 13,5k in 10000BC (5,6% share) to 235,8k in 1200AD (14,6% share, 1,59 inhabitants per km²). Its 251 catalogued archaeological sites — 74,7% of our entire settlement register, or 16,96 sites per 10.000 km² — reflect the unmatched spatial resolution of full-coverage pedestrian surveys across the Teotihuacán, Texcoco, Ixtapalapa, Chalco, Zumpango and Tula basins [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Millon1973; @Healan2012].

No other region experienced sharper oscillations in urban primacy. From Middle Formative lakeside hamlets such as Tlapacoya (1,7k) and early Chalco survey clusters, Late Formative nucleation raised Cuicuilco to 19,8k by 150BC alongside expanding Teotihuacán (28,5k by 100BC) [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Carballo2016]. Following the volcanic disruptions of Xitle and Popocatépetl, Teotihuacán absorbed a large share of regional population, reaching 96k in 250AD and 124k in 450AD — over half of the entire Basin of Mexico's Classic population packed into 20 km² [@Millon1973; @Cowgill2015]. Its satellite corridors stretched from Chingú (7,2k) on the Hidalgo lime flats to Texcoco Survey Site TX-CL-2 (9,6k) and Cholula (29,8k in 500AD) across the Sierra Nevada [@PlunketUrunuela2012].

After Teotihuacán's seventh-century collapse cut the city to 39,5k in 650AD and 11,8k by 1100AD, regional demographic momentum shifted outward rather than disappearing [@Cowgill2015; @Carballo2016]. Cantona expanded to 79,4k in 800AD on the eastern Puebla lava plateau; Xochicalco reached 15,6k in Morelos; Cacaxtla-Xochitécatl held 11,4k in Tlaxcala; Teotenango grew to 9,4k in Toluca; and Cholula rebounded to 33,2k by 1100AD [@PlunketUrunuela2012; @Carballo2016]. On the northern rim, Tula consolidated the Early Post-Classic Toltec realm at 56,4k in 1000AD and 44,8k in 1150AD, while northern basin communities such as Tizayuca maintained mixed agrarian and domestic-canid economies [@Mastache2002; @Healan2012; @Manin2018Identify]. By 1200AD, as Tula declined, lakeside Chalco (14,9k) and Culhuacán (9,4k) led the next cycle of Basin of Mexico nucleation, supporting an archaeological survey estimate of 2,45M inhabitants across the wider Central Highlands [@SandersParsonsSantley1979].

## Gulf Olmec Lowlands and Veracruz Littoral

The Gulf Olmec and Veracruz Lowlands (125.755,7 km², 7% of domain area) emerged in 1200AD as the highest-density sub-region in the gridded raster substratum at 1,84 inhabitants per km² (230,9k inhabitants, 14,3% share, a 10,97-fold rise from 21k in 10000BC), with 24 catalogued archaeological centres (1,91 sites per 10.000 km²). In the archaeological survey calibration envelope, its humid double-cropping floodplains climb from 320k in 1000BC to 720k in 600AD and 980k in 1200AD (8,16 inhabitants per km²).

Chronologically, the Gulf coast experienced two great demographic blooms separated by a long Late Formative reorganisation. The first was the Olmec surge along the Coatzacoalcos and Tonalá river systems, where San Lorenzo Tenochtitlán reached 10,8k in 1000BC, supported by dense river-levee hamlets in Capoacan and Medias Aguas, before La Venta attained 11,4k in 600BC and Tres Zapotes sustained 7,9k into the Classic era [@Diehl2004; @Pool2007; @Baizabal2019Asentamiento; @Reyes2019Patro]. Even then, lowland demographic stability remained sensitive to fluvial shifts and upland-lowland migration pulses [@Contributors2007Determinants].

The second bloom unfolded farther north in central and northern Veracruz during the Classic and Epiclassic centuries. Matacapan in the Tuxtla foothills grew to 14,6k by 650AD as a major ceramic-producing entrepôt with strong Teotihuacán architectural ties; Cerro de las Mesas (8,4k in 450AD) anchored the lower Papaloapan; El Pital (9,6k in 450AD) dominated the Nautla river terraces; and El Tajín surged to 19,8k by 850AD as the monumental heart of Classic Veracruz. By 1200AD, Early Post-Classic Cempoala (9,9k) and coastal Quiahuiztlán were rising along the central Veracruz littoral alongside interior piedmont gateways such as Tehuacán Viejo (8,4k), mirroring the broad rural hinterland structure documented across adjacent southern Gulf landscapes [@Stuardo2005Archaeological].

## Oaxaca and Mixteca Sierra-Valleys

Occupying just 60.535,6 km² (3,4% of total area), Oaxaca and Mixteca Sierra-Valleys achieved the second-highest gridded density by 1200AD at 1,61 inhabitants per km² (97,7k inhabitants, 6% share, up 17,1-fold from 5,7k in 10000BC) and the highest archaeological survey density in Mexico at 17,06 inhabitants per km² (960k inhabitants in 1200AD, up from 240k in 1000BC and 740k in 600AD). Fifteen catalogued settlements (2,48 sites per 10.000 km²) trace an unbroken sequence from Archaic Guilá Naquitz (62 occupants around 5000BC) through Classic statehood to Early Post-Classic confederation.

Valley circumscription and hilltop hydraulic engineering made Oaxaca a classic laboratory of early state demography [@Williams2025Testing; @Gracida2019Studying]. Monte Albán rose steadily from 5,3k in 450BC to 17,2k in 100AD, 21,6k in 400AD and 24,9k in 650AD, drawing artisans and tribute from terraced piedmonts across Etla, Tlacolula and Ocotlán [@Blanton1999; @Kowalewski1989; @Pachecofores2025Radiogenic]. Unlike the abrupt fiery rupture at Teotihuacán, Monte Albán's eighth-century decline redistributed Zapotec population across a polycentric network of valley capitals: Jalieza climbed to 16,2k in 950AD, Zaachila reached 9,6k by 1200AD, Yagul expanded to 6,9k in 1150AD and Lambityeco specialised in salt extraction [@Kowalewski1989]. Simultaneously, upland Mixteca Alta valleys at Yucuita and Huamelulpan, coastal Río Viejo (6,9k in 650AD) and Sierra Sur hilltop towns maintained vigorous autonomous trajectories into the Post-Classic world [@Geurds2008Grounding; @Zborover2014Decolonizing].

## West Mexico, the Bajío Frontier and the Arid North

West of the Central Highlands, West Mexico Santiago-Balsas (134.939 km², 7,6% of domain) expanded 9,3-fold in the gridded substratum from 19,7k in 10000BC to 182,7k in 1200AD (1,35 inhabitants per km², 11,3% share), while archaeological calibration places its fertile volcanic lake basins at 780k in 600AD and 1,22M in 1200AD (9,35 inhabitants per km²). Twelve catalogued sites (0,89 per 10.000 km²) highlight a shift from the circular-pyramid Teuchitlán core at Guachimontones (peaking at 22,4k in 400AD) toward Late Classic and Early Post-Classic regional centres including Loma Alta in Zacapu (7,6k in 1050AD), Ixtlán del Río Los Toriles (6,9k in 950AD), El Chanal (5,9k in 1150AD) and La Campana in Colima (5,4k in 700AD). Around Lake Pátzcuaro, expanding agricultural terrace systems stabilised fragile volcanic slopes and multiplied local carrying capacity ahead of the rise of the Post-Classic Tarascan state [@Pezzutti2007Steps].

North of the Lerma river, the Bajío and North-Central Highlands (285.316,5 km², 16% of area) displays a classic frontier advance-and-retreat curve. While gridded population climbs 5,1-fold from 56,8k in 10000BC to 289,4k in 1200AD (1,01 inhabitants per km²), archaeological calibration registers a Classic expansion peak of 390k in 600AD followed by a contraction to 340k in 1200AD as drying climates pushed northern Mesoamerican colonists back toward Tula and the Basin of Mexico [@Mastache2002]. Fourteen catalogued frontier centres — led by Tamtoc (6,9k), El Cerrito in Querétaro (6,9k), Amapa (6,4k), fortified La Quemada (4,9k in 750AD), El Teúl (4,3k) and Alta Vista Chalchihuites — mark the northernmost monumental stone architecture of the Classic era.

Farther northwest, Pacific Sierra Madre and Sonora-Sinaloa (83.542,3 km², 4,7% of area) grew 4,13-fold in the gridded series from 16,8k in 10000BC to 69,3k in 1200AD (0,83 inhabitants per km²), anchored by just three catalogued coastal river centres led by Early Aztatlán Culiacán (7k by 1200AD) and Chametla (4,5k). Finally, the immense Arid Northern Interior and Baja California (948.117,4 km², 53,1% of all land) remained the thinnest sub-region throughout every era: 0,54 inhabitants per km² in the 1200AD gridded series (513,8k, 31,7% share) and just 0,26 inhabitants per km² in the archaeological calibration series (240k). Its 17 catalogued sites (0,18 per 10.000 km²) trace both deep Archaic foraging persistence — Isla Cedros, Cuatro Ciénegas, Boca de Potrerillos and the Sierra de San Francisco rock-art shelters — and emerging Late Classic to Early Post-Classic desert farming oases at Guasave (2,5k), Huatabampo (1,7k), Cerro de Trincheras (1,6k) and Viejo-period Paquimé (1,5k).

## Urban Hierarchy and Rank-Size Scaling across 336 Settlements

Figure \ref{fig:meso-hierarchy} displays the twelve largest recorded settlements (Panel A) alongside the log-log rank-size distribution across all 336 catalogued city-proper sites (Panel B). Fitting the upper half of the settlement spectrum (168 sites) yields a steep, mature urban power-law exponent of $\alpha = 1,09$ ($R^2 = 0,88$), standing slightly above the classic Zipfian benchmark of $\alpha = 1$ and far above pre-urban foraging societies ($\alpha \approx 0,4$).

<img class="crd-figure-img" src="/artefacts/project_jaguar/1.0-precolumbian-mesoamerica/precolumbian_mesoamerica_urban_hierarchy.png" alt="fig:meso-hierarchy" loading="lazy" />
<figcaption class="crd-caption"><span class="crd-caption-label">Figure 3.</span> Twelve largest recorded Pre-Columbian settlements (Panel A) and rank-size power-law distribution across 336 catalogued settlements showing a mature urban slope ($\alpha = 1,09$, $R^2 = 0,88$, Panel B), 10000BC to 1200AD.</figcaption>
</figure>

Inspection of Panel B reveals a subtle concave shoulder below the power-law line at ranks 1 through 10 and a steeper tail drop-off beyond rank 100. That dual curvature has clear historical meaning. Because our chapter spans more than two millennia of successive urban empires rather than a single frozen census year, the top five capitals — Teotihuacán (124k in 450AD), Cantona (79,4k in 800AD), Tula (56,4k in 1000AD), Cholula (33,2k in 1100AD) and Monte Albán (24,9k in 650AD) — peaked in staggered chronological epochs, smoothing out single-century primate dominance when pooled across the full 10000BC to 1200AD window [@Millon1973; @Healan2012; @Kowalewski1989]. Conversely, the rapid drop below rank 100 reflects the dense tail of 231 ASU Basin of Mexico rural survey hamlets ranging from 30 to 1.500 residents that remain under-sampled in less intensively surveyed regions outside the central valleys. # Limitations

Five methodological constraints bound confidence in Pre-Columbian Mexican demographic estimates prior to 1200AD.

First, the tension between gridded global Holocene land-use substrata and regional archaeological pedestrian surveys cannot be glossed over. In our chapter summary cache, the gridded series drops sharply from 1,74M in 1000BC to 619,4k in 100AD before climbing to 1,62M in 1200AD, and allocates 31,7% of its 1200AD headcount to the Arid Northern Interior and Baja California. Regional archaeological surveys in the Basin of Mexico, Oaxaca, Veracruz and West Mexico instead support 4,93M inhabitants in 600AD and 6,65M by 1200AD with over four-fifths concentrated inside the four Mesoamerican basins [@SandersParsonsSantley1979; @Cowgill2015; @Kowalewski1989]. Both trajectories are reported transparently so downstream users understand how raster hindcasts under-weight pre-industrial highland urban density relative to field surveys.

Second, survey visibility and excavation intensity are intensely skewed toward the Basin of Mexico. Fully 251 of our 336 catalogued settlements (74,7%, or 16,96 sites per 10.000 km²) lie inside the Basin of Mexico and Central Highlands thanks to decades of full-coverage ASU survey work, compared with 2,48 sites per 10.000 km² in Oaxaca, 1,91 in the Gulf Olmec lowlands, 0,89 in West Mexico, 0,49 in the Bajío, 0,36 in Pacific Sierra Madre and 0,18 across the Arid North. Alluvial burial along the Coatzacoalcos, Papaloapan and Balsas floodplains hides Formative villages under metres of silt [@Pool2007; @Reyes2019Patro], while heavy volcanic ash mantles around Popocatépetl and Xitle conceal Formative rural landscapes [@PlunketUrunuela2012].

Third, translating mapped site area and surface sherd scatter into simultaneous living inhabitants carries wide parametric error bars ($\pm 25\%$ to $\pm 40\%$). Even at exhaustively mapped Teotihuacán, estimates for the 450AD peak span 80k to 125k depending on assumed household size per apartment compound and contemporaneous occupation fractions [@Millon1973; @Cowgill2015; @Carballo2010Advances]. At low-density Gulf and upland Oaxaca settlements, where patio groups sat amidst infield gardens and mountain terraces, surface sherd multipliers are still harder to standardise across ceramic phases [@Geurds2008Grounding; @Zborover2014Decolonizing].

Fourth, Archaic hunter-gatherer and Early Formative village populations before 1500BC leave scant architectural footprints. Radiocarbon clusters from dry shelters such as Guilá Naquitz and Coxcatlán Cave index selective cave preservation rather than open-air band density, and coastal Archaic shell middens along the Gulf and Pacific shelves suffered Holocene marine submergence.

Fifth, chronological phasing across regional ceramic sequences (such as Teotihuacán's Tlamimilolpa-Xolalpan phases versus Oaxaca's Monte Albán IIIA-IIIB or Veracruz's Remojadas horizons) introduces 50-to-150-year alignment uncertainties when aggregating continental totals at fixed centennial slices, while palaeodemographic mortality reconstructions remain uneven outside well-sampled skeletal series [@Morfin2013Mayas; @Contributors2007Determinants].

# Conclusion

Over the eleven millennia from 10000BC to 1200AD, Mexico outside the lowland Maya east underwent one of the world's great independent transitions from sparse Holocene foraging to dense, terraced and irrigated urban civilisation. Whether measured through the gridded Holocene substratum (rising 6,71-fold from 241,2k in 10000BC to 1,62M in 1200AD, with 1200AD densities led by the Gulf Lowlands at 1,84 inhabitants per km², Oaxaca at 1,61 and the Basin of Mexico at 1,59) or through bottom-up archaeological pedestrian surveys (climbing from 120k in 10000BC and 1,42M in 1000BC to 4,93M in 600AD and 6,65M by 1200AD), the structural trajectory is unmistakable [@Gonzalezmartin2015Demographic; @SandersParsonsSantley1979].

Domestication of maize, squash and beans in semi-arid southern highland shelters unlocked sedentary village life by 2000BC; alluvial wetland levees along the Gulf coast launched Mesoamerica's first monumental polities at San Lorenzo and La Venta [@Diehl2004; @Pool2007]; topographic circumscription and hilltop hydrology forged the Zapotec state at Monte Albán [@Blanton1999]; and volcanic displacement combined with intensive basin agriculture built Teotihuacán into a 124k planned metropolis unmatched in the ancient Americas [@Cowgill2015]. Even Teotihuacán's seventh-century fire did not reverse long-run demographic growth. Instead, Epiclassic realignment distributed urban vigour across Cantona, Cholula, El Tajín, Xochicalco, Jalieza and West Mexico, before Early Post-Classic Tula integrated central Mexico with retreating Bajío frontier colonists to set the stage for the densely packed city-states of the thirteenth through sixteenth centuries [@Mastache2002; @Healan2012].

# Footnotes

All population totals, settlement counts and sub-regional densities in Tables \ref{tab:subregion-trajectories} through \ref{tab:subregion-coverage} are computed dynamically from the chapter's cached demographic summary, archaeological calibration configuration, geocoded settlement register and source ledger. Calendar years follow astronomical sign conventions in underlying data tables (negative integers for BC, positive integers for AD), rendered in prose and table headers without thousands separators inside era labels (for example 10000BC, 600AD and 1200AD; year 0 in the raster grid is displayed as 1AD). Place names retain conventional Hispanic and indigenous diacritics in prose while remaining aligned with standardised ASCII identifiers in underlying cartographic layers.
